To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the historical records are so flawed that they do not allow a sound test of the hypothesis that propagule pressure is a key determinant of the success or failure of passerine introduces to New Zealand; (2) the analysis of Blackburn et al. (2011 ) is biased in favour of this hypothesis; (3) the population viability analysis used to support this hypothesis is based on unjustifiable and questionable assumptions; (4) the outcome of introductions was likely determined by species
(1) the propagule pressure effect is not supported for passerine birds introduced to New Zealand and (2) the propagule size effect is not supported either.

(a) the historical record of passerine introduces to New Zealand is so flawed that we cannot determine the factors that caused some species to become established, and (b) our re-analysis of the data does not provide support for the propagule pressure theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms behind successful bird introductions to islands.
the validity of the propagule hypothesis, not the accuracy of the historical record of bird introductions.
the validity of Blackburn et al.’s (2011) claim of a support for the propagule pressure theory.

propagule pressure was not the only factor influencing success or failure of passerine introduces to New Zealand.
we have no idea what caused the success or failure of passerine bird species following introduction to New Zealand.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we do not know the mechanisms of success and failure for introduced passerines, and that the propagule pressure idea is a poor substitute for a comprehensive analysis.
we have found no evidence that the propagule pressure concept can be used to understand the success and failure of passerine introduces to New Zealand.
we have no idea what the outcome of bird introductions to NZ depended on.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the historical record is too poor to draw firm conclusions about the relative importance of propagule pressure versus other factors.
the historical record of passerine bird introduction to New Zealand is too flawed to be used as a test of the propagule hypothesis.
the historical record of New Zealand passerine introductions is so flawed that it is not a useful test of any hypothesis about the causes of extinction following introduction.
